entries.title: Sydney Sweeney has great jeans. Who made them? (Psst: Workers)
entries.summary: Sydney Sweeney has great jeans, American Eagle Outfitters tells us. But who made them? And what are working conditions like in the garment factories of Pakistan and Bangladesh?
entries.content:
Sydney Sweeney has great jeans. Who made them? (Psst: Workers)

KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters advertisement playing on a smartphone.

But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.

When Sweeney's advertisement for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)

Missing from the debate over whether the advertisement was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.

The workers who make Sydney Sweeney's jeans

Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."

S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.

She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.

Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.

In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."

S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladeshand Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.

Inside the world of fast fashion

Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.

The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.

These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.

It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd, executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes. "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."

"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.

Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that those factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid." 

H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.

Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."

One worker's survival strategy

Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.

R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."

R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."

So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.

R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.

MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.

Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.

Taking the heat

These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.

Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh  to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.

There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.

Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."

But for now, workers in Pakistan, in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi, one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.

In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.

In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.

One young woman worker is I.

Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.

I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.

She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"

Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.

Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.

A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."

Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA, a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.

Answers from fast fashion brands

NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.

Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."

Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners, which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.

Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."

H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."

Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."

Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.

Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.

Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."

With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
entries.summary: Officials are seeking at least $1 million in damages from the owners of the tanker that hit a cruise ship last week. The incident was dubbed "the miracle on the Mississippi" after no one was killed.
entries.content:
New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management as defendants.

The lawsuit states that at 12:30 p.m. Friday, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat which was docked at the Thalia Street terminal for disembarkment of passengers.

There were almost 200 people on board the American Heritage at the time of the crash, which left the ship on its side and partially submerged. All passengers and crew survived, including more than 100 who were rescued from the river, leading New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno to dub the incident "the miracle on the Mississippi."

There were 32 people brought to the hospital, none with critical injuries.

The port commissioners said as a result of the collision, the Thalia Street terminal had significant damage.

"The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed [$1 million], with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated," the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit also states that the port expects to incur additional costs, including clean-up, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs.

On Friday, port officials requested the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs of the damage. A federal judge approved the seizure request.

Officials claimed that the collision occurred "as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" by Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping SA and Thome Ship Management.

Clearing the Mississippi

As of Saturday, eight people remained in the hospital, two in serious condition.

Mayor Moreno said Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed away from the site, but noted it could take weeks to fully remove the American Heritage.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said that operations were now focused on fully reopening the river and safe removal of hazardous material on board the American Heritage. Burnham said it is estimated there are 160,000 gallons of fuel on board the ship.

"We're going to have divers in the water so they can do a full assessment on what's the right path to be able to remove it," Burnham said. "We also have teams that have been deployed throughout the entire area, the river system to monitor the area for any pollution."

Burnham said there are restrictions in place for boat traffic along the Mississippi River.

The exact cause of the crash is unknown, though Burnham said the tanker appeared to have an issue with steering. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

John DeLeeuw, board member with the NTSB, said during a Saturday briefing that the tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered.

"The voyage data recorder essentially is going to provide the data," DeLeeuw said. "It's like a flight data recorder on an aircraft. We can look at speeds and all kinds of information. It's essentially covering speed all kinds of maneuverings that was done on the ship."

A preliminary report by the NTSB is expected within 30 days, with the final report on probable causes and safety recommendations coming in 18 to 24 months.

entries.title: Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back
entries.summary: Coal miners who are exposed to silica dust are at a higher risk of black lung disease. Despite decades of advocacy, new efforts to regulate the toxic dust are under threat.
entries.content:
Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back

Coal miners who are exposed to silica dust are at a higher risk of black lung disease. Despite decades of advocacy, new efforts to regulate the toxic dust are under threat.

AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

An epidemic of an incurable disease among coal miners in Appalachia got new attention this past Tuesday. Federal regulators propose major changes in the rules that are supposed to protect miners from black lung disease. Our former NPR colleague Howard Berkes has been reporting on this since 2011. His new "Frontline" PBS film, "Coal's Human Cost," also came out Tuesday. He joins me now to discuss the film and the difficulties in regulating the mining industry. Thank you so much for being here, Howard.

HOWARD BERKES: It's good to be with you, Ayesha.

RASCOE: For many people, black lung disease sounds like something out of the dark days of coal mining a hundred years ago. Why is there still an epidemic of black lung disease?

BERKES: Because the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out in recent decades, and mining companies turned to much thinner strips of coal. And they're embedded in rock, and so the mining machines pulverize rock as they cut into coal. That results in very fine, easily inhaled particles of highly toxic silica, which cause severe scarring and stiffness in the lungs.

RASCOE: I mean, that just sounds horrible. Before we get to that human cost you focused on in the film, what rule changes did the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration propose Tuesday?

BERKES: You know, this goes back actually to 2024 when the Biden administration imposed strict limits on silica dust and, for the first time, direct enforcement. The changes proposed on Tuesday give mining companies more control over monitoring silica dust because, the agency says, mine operators have 40 years of experience. But, you know, that experience hasn't prevented thousands of cases of disease, and the rate of disease now among some miners is back to what it was in 1978. So the bottom line for mining advocates is that the proposed changes make enforcement weaker.

RASCOE: What does the failure of mining companies and federal regulators to keep miners safe look like on the ground?

BERKES: I met miner Tim Balthis in Virginia. He was diagnosed five years ago with the advanced stage of disease.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

TIM BALTHIS: The death is real. That's going to happen. If the rest of my body stays in good shape and I don't get killed in a car accident or something like that, I'm going to die of black lung. I know that. With the diagnosis that I have, I'll probably be lucky to live into mid-60s.

BERKES: How old are you now?

BALTHIS: I will be 58 in November.

BERKES: Mid-60s isn't far off.

BALTHIS: No. No, it's not.

RASCOE: Your film also steps back in time a bit and revisits some scenes from another film of yours eight years ago. Why did you do that?

BERKES: We wanted to show how little has changed since then, so we talked to some of the same people we featured back then. That includes Ron Carson, the now-retired director of the Stone Mountain black lung clinics in Virginia.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

RON CARSON: For us to be sitting here discussing what we are talking about over the past eight years and nothing's been done - it just - it's horrifying. It's just horrifying, 'cause we put the data out there. We put the facts out there. And something should have been done on a higher level to make sure that we wouldn't be here today talking about this.

RASCOE: Howard, like, is there no hope for minors with this disease, no treatment? Maybe lung transplants, for example - could that help them?

BERKES: There really is no cure, but one of the miners we featured in the film did have one of those double lung transplants five years ago. Greg Kelly described for us how difficult that surgery was.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

GREG KELLY: The surgeon, when he talked to me - he said, I had to scrape your lungs out. He said, I couldn't even pick them up. He said, that's how bad they was. He said, you cold miners are extremely tough to do lung transplants on.

BERKES: That's how bad these miners' lungs get. Now, lung transplants for coal miners are rare, and recovery isn't easy. Greg Kelly is one serious infection away from losing his new life. He's thrilled that he's had five more years. But the median life expectancy for a minor with a lung transplant is just 6 1/2 years.

RASCOE: Yeah. That's really tough to go through. With this new proposed regulation, like, what's ahead for coal miners?

BERKES: Lawsuits are certain for the regulation. It'll likely be months, and maybe longer, before the new regulation is final. And in the meantime, the tougher regulation that the Biden administration put in place is on hold indefinitely. So miners today have the same protections that failed so many of them in the past.

RASCOE: Howard Berkes, thank you so much for joining us.

BERKES: Thank you, Ayesha.

RASCOE: The film "Coal's Human Cost" from the PBS program "Frontline" is now available for streaming on YouTube and at pbs.org.

entries.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
entries.summary: In several states, Democrats took control of legislatures that had been divided and they weakened GOP dominance in others. Issues on the agenda: More access to health care, new limits on school vouchers.
entries.content:
Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures

Democrats made gains in legislatures across the country

The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.

Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years. The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years.

The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.

Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18. The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.

So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.

The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.

New Democratic 'trifectas,' controlling the legislature and governor's office

The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.

The president of their rival organization, Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."

Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."

In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.

One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program, which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.

In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.

Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)

Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states

In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.

Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.

Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.

North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.

In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.

That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

Colin Campbell of WUNC, Sarah Kallis of Georgia Public Broadcasting, Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of WHYY and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ, contributed to this story.

entries.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
entries.summary: A year ago in November, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every eligible family, regardless of income.
entries.content:
New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.

"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."

A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.

Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.

"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.

There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.

When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.

"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.

Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.

"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."

According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.

But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.

In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.

Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.

Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center, said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."

"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."

But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.

The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.

How it happened in New Mexico

Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.

Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.

Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.

Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.

"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.

The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."

"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.

But she knows more capacity is needed.

"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."

In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.

A nationwide childcare shortage

It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.

Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. That's one reason she's part of a group chat that includes over 40 childcare providers in her area.

"Every time somebody calls me, you know, I put their name and the age of their kids in that group. And I'm like, 'Does anybody have openings?' You know, but the sad thing is that not a lot of people have openings, especially for infants."

Grays, a single mother of five, operates out of her home in Las Cruces, in the southern part of the state.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. The outdoor space is part children's playground and part garden oasis.

"[The children] can play with water, with dirt, grass. They ground themselves. It makes a world of a difference," Grays said.

She wishes she didn't have to turn any children away.

"I think that's one of our biggest issues right now, is making sure that we have enough spots available for everybody coming in," Grays said. "And I think that's one of the flaws that perhaps other states can learn from."

According to the Center for American Progress, rural areas especially struggle with childcare deserts — and New Mexico is very rural.

"It's not a lack of funding, it's a lack of providers," the state's speaker of the house, Javier Martinez, told NPR. He's a Democrat and an advocate for universal childcare. "We have communities that are miles from any type of population center. Hundreds of miles sometimes. And so there are communities where that market isn't quite there to support a business."

The tension around providing free childcare to wealthier families

The program's current operating budget is almost $600 million.

But there's concern among some state lawmakers that it's projected to be about $50 million over budget this year.

"By calling it universal, all we've done is add the wealthier folks," said state Sen. Steve Lanier, a Republican representing the northwest corner of New Mexico.

Lanier sued to stop the governor's universal childcare initiative — a lawsuit that was ultimately unsuccessful.

He told NPR that the steep price tag for this program is why he only supports childcare assistance for some.

"My daughter's a school teacher. She has two young boys. She gets free childcare. So, from a personal view, I see where it is needed. I mean, that helps her and her family immensely," Lanier said. "But somebody that's making $450,000, $600,000, do they really need that assistance?"

Catron Allred, who oversees the early childhood center at Santa Fe Community College, doesn't see it that way.

"To me, I think it's a mentality of early childhood as a public good," she explained. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood."

It's not a one-size-fits-all model

While New Mexico is the only state with free, universal childcare right now, other states and cities have made progress in that direction, including Oregon, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., New York City and Vermont, which has tapped into payroll taxes for funding.

In New York City, which already has free prekindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds, Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently rolled out free daycare for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds.

As in New Mexico, "Both the biggest challenge and opportunity in New York City is our scale," explained Emmy Liss, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

"We know that every family's childcare needs are different. We know that our diverse landscape of childcare providers offer a really wide mix of services that families value," Liss added. "But to build a system that incorporates all of those different providers and meets the needs of all of our families is a complex challenge."

Liss said the goal is to have free pre-k for every 2-year-old by the end of the mayor's first term. But instead of expanding access to everyone all at once, as New Mexico has done, she said the city is growing capacity "in parallel" with access by creating more slots and matching them with families.

"We are working to build the infrastructure, the workforce, the physical capacity and the support to providers to ensure that we can continue to scale access to care here," Liss told NPR.

She said her office has been in conversation with leaders in New Mexico, and has had the chance to learn from them. But ultimately, she said, "Our realities are different."

"I think we're making slightly different choices in how we are implementing expanded access to care, which is good. I think we should be making different choices, responsive to the needs we hear from New Yorkers."

Childcare can make or break a parent's work life

Veronica Ramirez lives in Ohkay Owingeh, a federally recognized tribe and pueblo in northern New Mexico. She said she learned about universal childcare when it was in the news last year and decided to enroll her 2-year-old daughter.

"For my daughter, I think it's really opened doors for her," Ramirez told NPR.

"Just being able to be around other little human beings that are her age...I've seen her go up to other little kids in public and say hi or just start playing with them. And I'm like, 'Oh, well, she's social now. She's not clinging to mom only.' "

For Ramirez, having consistent childcare has enabled her to do more nonprofit work, including as an outreach coordinator at a birth center that primarily serves indigenous clients in nearby Española. It helps that her 7-year-old son is in school for the same hours as her daughter is in daycare.

"Now I'm able to work more and make more money and support my family a little bit better," Ramirez said.

The childcare help has opened other doors for her, too.

"I'm trying to get my bachelor's. I had my son when I was 19, right when I graduated high school," Ramirez said. "It's taken me a little bit longer, but I'm getting closer to getting a degree."

A new paper from Arizona State University found that lower-income mothers in New Mexico have seen significant gains since free, universal childcare was enacted, with full-time employment increasing by 23%.

But for Lilia Doyle, in Santa Fe, working full-time won't be an option until she gets her son off a waitlist and into consistent childcare. When she first spoke to NPR in September, she said she and her family are living on her husband's income.

"Hopefully our finances will be able to absorb it," she said. "We'll buckle down, and we'll make it through, but … it's not ideal."

Then, in October, Doyle got some news: A childcare center told her they found a spot for her son – but it wouldn't open up until August 2027.

entries.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
entries.summary: The film Being Heumann tells the lesser-known story of the mother of the disability rights movement. A new generation of activists share how they "carry the torch" today.
entries.content:
A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy

Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.

Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Siân Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.

Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.

But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.

Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."

With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.

"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.

Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.

As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."

Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.

These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.

On what stood out most about Being Heumann:

Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.

Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.

Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.

Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.

On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:

Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.

Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.

Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."

On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:

Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.

Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.

Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?

Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie

Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

entries.title: Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal
entries.summary: A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House.
entries.content:
Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge after she ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

entries.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
entries.summary: Some college football games were delayed a few hours on Saturday or postponed to Sunday. And in Oklahoma at least, there will be perks for fans to make up for the inconvenience, including cheap beers.
entries.content:
FAA ground stop disrupts college football

The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

entries.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
entries.summary: A new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives has prompted Delray Beach to cancel its St. Patrick's Day parade after a nearly 60-year run.
entries.content:
Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

entries.title: Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary
entries.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy points blame toward contractor in explaining Friday's nation-wide aviation ground stop.
entries.content:
Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground stop, says Transportation Secretary

Maintenance gone awry caused nation-wide ground, says Transportation Secretary

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy points blame toward contractor in explaining Friday's nation-wide aviation ground stop.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

What caused the cascade of failures which brought the U.S. air travel system to its knees on Friday? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation - a contractor was replacing a router to upgrade the nation's outdated air traffic control equipment when something went very wrong.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

SEAN DUFFY: This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment. Our contractor didn't meet the moment. Or the equipment didn't meet the moment and cause the outages.

SCHMITZ: The system is back online, and flights are now taking off, but travelers throughout the country are still dealing with the disruption. NPR spoke to one traveler, Andres Martinez Murillo, last night.

ANDRES MARTINEZ MURILLO: My flight keeps getting delayed further. They don't know if it's, like, a crew issue. They don't know if it's, like, a pilot issue. I don't even know if we have a plane.

SCHMITZ: Murillo told NPR he finally boarded his first flight this morning, but his second flight's been canceled, and he still does not know when he will reach his final destination. For more, we're joined by NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose. Hey, Joel.

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Hey, Rob.

SCHMITZ: So many angry passengers today that still have not gotten to their destinations - what more do we know about the cause of all of this?

ROSE: We are starting to get a clearer picture. The heads of the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration held a press conference today, and they put the blame squarely on a longtime FAA contractor, L3 Harris Technologies. They say the company was doing a routine maintenance upgrade of a server as part of a transition from older copper wire to fiber optic cable, and that is when things went sideways.

Sean Duffy and FAA leaders were asked several times why a faulty router could lead to telecom outages across such a wide part of the country. They said that is still under investigation. In a statement, L3 Harris says it is supporting the FAA's investigation into what went wrong and that it takes the impact on airlines and travelers seriously.

SCHMITZ: OK. Let's step back here just for a moment. What was happening in the air while all of this was playing out on the ground?

ROSE: Air traffic controllers were starting to see intermittent problems with radar and communication systems around 3:30 p.m. Eastern. By 3:44 p.m., the FAA declared a nationwide ground stop. Here is some of the reaction from air traffic controllers and pilots in Salt Lake City, as you can hear in archived audio from the website, liveatc.net.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: You guys got any updates from your company about what's going on?

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Not at all. If you've got info, we're all ears.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: I wish we did. We basically only know what the FAA tells us, which is not a lot.

ROSE: I talked to one air traffic controller who was working when the outage began. He is a controller at one of the en route centers that handle high altitude traffic and was not authorized to speak publicly, but he described the situation as chaos. He said, a lot of airplanes were being diverted away from their original destinations. Some of them were running out of fuel. And he emphasized just how this whole system depends on the air traffic controllers, who found a way to more than 3,000 planes onto the ground quickly and safely, even when their equipment was letting them down.

SCHMITZ: So we've got a lot of confused pilots, a lot of confused air traffic controllers. You know, I'm just curious, the air traffic controller that you spoke to - did he have any thoughts about the apparent cause of this ground stop?

ROSE: I should say that we spoke this morning before the press conference by DOT, but this controller was already beginning to think that this was probably a mistake by a contractor who was doing work to upgrade the air traffic control system, which this controller says is happening all the time. He also places some of the blame on the oversight of the FAA for not having enough redundant systems in place, you know, to prevent this kind of outage from happening. He questioned why this work was going on in the middle of a busy Friday afternoon instead...

SCHMITZ: Right.

ROSE: ...Of late at night when it would not have had as much impact if something went wrong. He said it, quote, "just screams incompetence, like, gross incompetence."

SCHMITZ: You know, it does seem quite remarkable that a single point of failure like this could have such an enormous impact. What has the FAA said about this?

ROSE: Well, they said this was considered routine maintenance work. They are still investigating why it appears to have basically broken the entire national airspace. Here is Rebecca Guy, the acting chief technology officer at the FAA.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

REBECCA GUY: What we are doing is that root cause analysis, but at this time, we do believe what occurred with that router has been worked through.

ROSE: In other words, they think they have solved the problem. The FAA administrator promised that things should be back to normal by close of business on Sunday.

SCHMITZ: That is NPR transportation correspondent, Joel Rose. Joel, thank you so much for all that reporting.

ROSE: You're welcome.
